land: Ice ages now come roughly every 100,000 years. In the Anglian glaciation (about 478,000–424,000 years ago) ice reaches north London and the Isles of Scilly, the farthest south of any ice age, and pushes the Thames into its present course. Around 450,000 years ago a lake dammed by the ice bursts through the chalk ridge at Dover, the first step towards island Britain. The long, warm Hoxnian interglacial follows (about 424,000–374,000 years ago).
nature: In warm spells Europe has forest and open woodland with straight-tusked elephants, two kinds of rhinoceros, wild horses, giant deer, Barbary macaques, lions and jaguars. Aurochs, which first appeared in Africa, reach Italy by about 500,000 years ago. Woolly mammoths with fully cold-adapted teeth appear in Siberia about 400,000 years ago.
life: Archaic humans, often grouped as Homo heidelbergensis (a debated name), live in Africa and Europe, while Homo erectus lives on in East and Southeast Asia. At Boxgrove in England (about 480,000 years ago) people butcher horses and rhinos on a tidal flat with finely made hand-axes. At Sima de los Huesos in Spain, about 430,000 years ago, the bodies of about 29 people end up in a deep cave shaft; their DNA puts them on the Neanderthal line.
living: People hunt and scavenge big animals and shape hand-axes with soft hammers of antler and elephant bone. Fire becomes common between 400,000 and 300,000 years ago: hearths at Beeches Pit (England) and Qesem Cave (Israel), and at Barnham in Suffolk the oldest evidence of making fire, with flint and pyrite, about 400,000 years ago. Stone points at Kathu Pan in South Africa (about 500,000 years ago) may have tipped spears.
disease: Almost nothing is known about infections. Violence is visible: one skull from Sima de los Huesos has two matching blows to the forehead, probably from the same weapon. Groups are tiny and scattered, so crowd diseases cannot persist.
soc: Almost nothing is known about group life. Genetic models suggest the ancestors of modern humans had earlier passed through a severe bottleneck, about 930,000–813,000 years ago, of no more than about 1,280 breeding individuals (Hu 2023, debated). The Sima de los Huesos dead are mostly young adults who seem to have died at about the same time; a single unused quartzite hand-axe (“Excalibur”) lay with them, possibly an offering (debated).

land: Glacial cycles continue: a cold stage until about 243,000 years ago, a warm one, then the long Saalian glaciation (about 191,000–130,000 years ago), when ice reaches as far south as Düsseldorf. A second megaflood through the Dover Strait about 160,000 years ago removes the last of the chalk ridge, so from now on Britain becomes an island whenever the sea is high.
nature: With each swing of climate, cold-steppe and temperate-woodland animals trade places across Europe. At Schöningen in Germany, wild horses are hunted at a lakeshore whose fauna also includes red deer, steppe bison, aurochs, two kinds of rhinoceros, straight-tusked elephants and sabre-toothed cats.
life: The oldest known Homo sapiens fossils, from Jebel Irhoud in Morocco (about 315,000 years ago, debated), have modern faces but long, low braincases. Neanderthals take shape in Europe and Denisovans in Asia, known from Denisova Cave in Siberia and a jaw from Xiahe on the Tibetan Plateau (over 160,000 years old). Small-brained Homo naledi lives in South Africa (about 335,000–236,000 years ago). Modern humans reach the Levant at Misliya (about 185,000 years ago) and perhaps Greece at Apidima (about 210,000, debated).
living: Across Africa the Middle Stone Age begins, with prepared-core (Levallois) flakes and stone spear points; at Olorgesailie in Kenya, about 320,000 years ago, people carry obsidian over long distances and use red pigment. At Schöningen people make spruce throwing spears up to 2.5 m long (once dated to about 300,000 years ago, re-dated in 2025 to about 200,000). At Pinnacle Point in South Africa people gather shellfish and use ochre by about 165,000 years ago.
disease: There are signs of care for the sick. A Neanderthal child with inner-ear changes typical of Down syndrome, from Cova Negra in Spain, lived to at least six, which would have needed help from the group (date uncertain, within 273,000–146,000 years ago).
soc: Very little is known. Genetic models put early Homo sapiens at about 100,000–300,000 people around 200,000 years ago (Sjödin 2012, an estimate). Several human species share the planet. Homo naledi bodies were placed deep in a South African cave system, possibly as burials (strongly debated). At Jebel Irhoud, butchered gazelle bones and burned flints mark a hunting camp around a fire.

land: A warm interglacial, at times about 2 °C warmer than today, peaking about 128,000–123,000 years ago. Seas stand 6–9 m higher than now as the Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets shrink, and Britain is an island. Rains are stronger than in the Holocene, turning the Sahara and Arabia green.
nature: Hippos live in the Thames: their bones lie under Trafalgar Square with those of lions, rhinos and straight-tusked elephants, and hippos reach as far north as the River Tees. Forest grows up to North Cape in Norway, oak and hazel as far as Oulu in Finland, and boreal forest on the coast of Alaska.
life: Neanderthals live across Europe and western Asia. At Krapina in Croatia (about 130,000 years ago) they keep eight white-tailed eagle talons, cut, polished and probably worn together as jewellery. Modern humans live in the Levant at Skhul, and stone tools at Jebel Faya in Arabia (about 125,000 years ago) suggest people crossing a greener Arabia. In Java the last known Homo erectus live at Ngandong (about 117,000–108,000 years ago).
living: Neanderthals camp in rock shelters and caves, hunt large game with wooden spears and stone points, and use fire routinely. Their prepared-core stone tools are made with the Levallois method. Modern humans in the Levant wear perforated sea shells, carried from a coast tens of kilometres away.
disease: Most Neanderthals die young: of 206 studied, about 80% of those who reached 20 died before 40, and an estimated 43% of infants died in northern Eurasia. Healed fractures and wounds are common.
soc: Neanderthal groups are small and thinly spread: their genetic effective population is about 3,000–12,000, and their total numbers perhaps 5,000–70,000 at any one time (Bocquet-Appel & Degioanni 2013, an estimate). At Krapina the bones of at least 23 people were broken and cut, read either as cannibalism or as cleaning bones for burial (debated).

land: The Last Glacial Period begins about 115,000 years ago. Ice grows in steps, interrupted by milder spells peaking around 96,000 and 82,000 years ago, until a sharp cold stage from about 71,000 years ago. About 74,000 years ago Toba in Sumatra produces the largest eruption in over two million years, spreading about 5 cm of ash across India.
nature: In the north, forest gives way to steppe and tundra as the cold returns. Woolly mammoths cross into North America about 100,000 years ago. On Flores, dwarf Stegodon (an elephant relative), Komodo dragons and giant rats share the island with small humans.
life: Modern humans in southern Africa make symbols: at Blombos Cave they mix ochre in abalone shells (about 100,000 years ago), wear shell beads and draw a cross-hatched pattern (about 73,000 years ago). Homo floresiensis, about 1.1 m tall, lives on Flores and Homo luzonensis on Luzon. A hand stencil on Muna Island near Sulawesi, at least 67,800 years old and probably made by modern humans, is the oldest known cave art.
living: In Africa people spear catfish with barbed bone harpoons (Katanda, about 90,000 years ago), glue stone tips onto handles (Sibudu, by about 70,000) and engrave ostrich-eggshell water containers (Diepkloof, about 60,000). In the Levant they bury their dead; at Qafzeh (about 95,000 years ago) a teenager lies with red deer antlers clasped to the chest, and ochre lies nearby.
disease: Toba may have cooled the climate for a few years (up to about 3.5 °C in models). The idea that it nearly wiped out humanity is now widely doubted: stone tools in southern India look the same above and below the ash.
soc: Older people are rare: the ratio of older to younger adults rises sharply only among modern humans after about 45,000 years ago (Caspari & Lee 2004; the method is debated). Neanderthals bury some of their dead: at Shanidar in Iraq a woman in her mid-40s or older was laid in a hand-dug gully over 70,000 years ago. A Toba “bottleneck” of 1,000–10,000 people (Ambrose 1998) is not supported by later evidence.

s: Middle of the Last Glacial · MIS 3
land: After the cold peak of MIS 4 the climate stays cold but unstable, with short warm spells every few thousand years. Seas are far below today’s level, so Australia, New Guinea and Tasmania form one continent, Sahul, and only narrow sea gaps separate it from Asia.
nature: Most of Australia’s giant animals disappear, mostly around 46,000 years ago: the hippo-sized Diprotodon, the marsupial lion, the giant short-faced kangaroo, the giant lizard Megalania and the flightless bird Genyornis. Whether people, climate or both are to blame is debated. In Eurasia the mammoth steppe feeds mammoths, woolly rhinos and cave lions.
life: Modern humans leave Africa in a lasting dispersal (about 70,000–50,000 years ago) and spread across Asia to Australia by about 50,000 years ago (65,000 at Madjedbebe, debated). They reach France briefly at Grotte Mandrin about 54,000 years ago and spread through Europe from about 45,000. On the way they interbreed with Neanderthals (about 50,500–43,500 years ago) and Denisovans. On Sulawesi, a painted scene of people and a pig is at least 51,200 years old.
living: Modern humans reach Sahul through a chain of sea crossings, the oldest known voyages. Neanderthal bands are small: in Chagyrskaya Cave in the Altai, a father and his teenage daughter lived together about 54,000 years ago. Neanderthals in Iraq bury their dead at Shanidar.
disease: Neanderthals show signs of inbreeding: up to a third of the Chagyrskaya genomes consist of long identical stretches. Mixing passes genes, some harmful, into modern humans; selection later removes many of them. An early European from Oase in Romania (about 40,000 years ago) carried up to 9% Neanderthal DNA, against about 2% in people today.
soc: Neanderthals live in groups of perhaps 10–20 people, with women moving between groups and men staying (Skov 2022). Shanidar 1 in Iraq lived on blind in one eye, nearly deaf and with a withered arm, suggesting others looked after him. Papuans and other Melanesians still carry about 4–6% Denisovan DNA, and all non-Africans about 2% Neanderthal DNA.
